title: Arrows of prayer (II.13)
hookLine: a whistle, a bark, rain on hot pavement: Francis de Sales thought any of them could start a two-second prayer
tomorrow: abuela's too weak for Mass. can she be there from bed?

lines: A WHISTLE. A BARK. RAIN ON HOT PAVEMENT.
cards: The whistle at the end of a drill. A dog barking two yards over. Rain hitting a hot parking lot, and that smell coming up off it.
Francis de Sales thought moments like these could start a prayer, and the prayer could be over before the light turns green. So what do you say in two seconds? A word.
Maybe three. He calls them aspirations, and he pictures them flying up like arrows.

teach.h: SHORT, WARM, MANY TIMES A DAY.
teach.b: First, what they are. Aspirations, Francis says, are short, warm movements of the heart toward God, sent many times a day. Admire his goodness, ask for help, thank him, give him your heart, all in a breath.
Second, the words are free. He ties you to no formula.

Use whatever words your heart finds, a phrase from the psalms, or simply the name of Jesus. One psalm line sits in the Douay-Rheims like this: "O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me."
Third, where they start. People in love, Francis says, keep coming back to the one they love, in thought and in word.

teach.h: A FLOWER, A VIEW, A KINDNESS.
teach.b: And almost anything the senses meet can set one off: a view, a flower, a small kindness, turned into a short word lifted to God. Fourth, how much weight he gives them.

In this exercise, the heart's retreat together with aspirations, he says, lies the great work of devotion. It can make up for other prayers that go missing, but hardly anything can make up for its loss.
The hour of prayer is the root.
The arrows keep the whole day in the air.

how: Some Catholics pray short lines through the day, such as the name of Jesus, a verse from the psalms, or a phrase like "Jesus, I trust in you"; older prayer books collect them as aspirations.

o: a short prayer of the heart, sent up in a moment
a deep breath taken to calm the mind
a big hope or ambition for the years ahead

games.q: your little cousin asks why abuela whispers something every time an ambulance goes past. from today's lesson, what's the best guess?
o: a short prayer, sparked by what she sees, sent up in a moment.
a saying to keep bad luck away from the house.
the start of a long prayer she has to finish later.
games.why: Francis says almost anything seen can start an aspiration: a few words from the heart, over in a breath.

practice: Let your eyes land on five things around you, one at a time: a window, a cup, your own hand, whatever is there. Stay with each for a few breaths, and let one short word rise from it: thanks, help, or a name.
If you pray, send those words to God.

wordCard.voice: Aspiration. A short prayer of the heart, sent up in a moment, many times a day.

orig.note: Latin: aspiration. Francis wrote in French, pairing aspirations with ejaculatory prayers.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: short arrows, small enough to fit between any two things you do. Until tomorrow.
